title: PMS fee structures, with a worked example
objectives: Work through the ₹1 crore up-year and down-year example.
body_md:
PMS fees are set in the agreement and usually take one of three forms: fixed (a flat % of assets a year), performance-linked (a share of profits above a hurdle rate, usually with a high-water mark), or hybrid (a lower fixed fee plus a profit share). Operating expenses, excluding brokerage, are capped at 0.5% a year.

Illustration on a ₹1 crore portfolio (hypothetical, before GST, brokerage and operating expenses):

| Year's gross return | Option A: 2.5% fixed | Option B: 1% fixed + 20% of gains above a 10% hurdle |
|---|---|---|
| +18% (₹18 L gain) | Fee ₹2.5 L → net gain ₹15.5 L | Fee ₹1 L + 20% of ₹8 L = ₹2.6 L → net gain ₹15.4 L |
| −10% (₹10 L loss) | Fee ₹2.5 L → net loss ₹12.5 L | Fee ₹1 L, no profit share → net loss ₹11 L |

The high-water mark means that after a loss year, the profit share is charged only on gains above the portfolio's previous peak, so the client does not pay twice for recovering the same ground.
example: On ₹1 crore after a +18% year, Option A (2.5% fixed) leaves a net gain of ₹15.5 lakh and Option B (1% fixed + 20% above a 10% hurdle) leaves ₹15.4 lakh. In a −10% year, A loses ₹12.5 lakh and B loses ₹11 lakh.
say: Here's exactly what you'd pay in fees in a good year and a bad year.
The high-water mark means you don't pay twice for recovering the same ground.
never: Performance fees are charged on every gain regardless of earlier losses.

talk_track.title: Fees, shown in rupees, in good and bad years
talk_track.text: Clients understand fees in rupees, not percentages, so always show them this way. Take a one crore portfolio and two fee options. Option A charges a flat 2.5% a year. Option B charges 1% fixed plus 20% of gains above a 10% hurdle. In a good year, with an 18% gross return, they cost almost the same: two and a half lakh versus two point six lakh, leaving a net gain of about fifteen and a half lakh either way. But in a bad year, with a 10% fall, Option A still charges two and a half lakh, while Option B charges only the one lakh fixed fee. So the client loses twelve and a half lakh with A, and eleven lakh with B. Neither is always better; what matters is that the client sees both years before choosing. This is a hypothetical example, before GST, brokerage and operating expenses.

talk_track.title: How a high-water mark protects the client
talk_track.text: When a PMS charges a share of profits, ask whether it uses a high-water mark, and explain it like this. Say a client's portfolio grows from one crore to one crore twenty lakh in year one. That's a new peak, so the manager earns a profit share. In year two it falls back to one crore, and in year three it recovers to one fifteen. With a high-water mark, no profit share is charged in those years, because the client is only regaining lost ground. In year four it reaches one thirty-five, and the profit share applies only to the fifteen lakh above the old peak of one twenty. Without a high-water mark, the client could pay twice for the same gains. Always check the agreement for when and how the high-water mark resets.

check.why: In a down year A still charges ₹2.5 L, while B charges only its ₹1 L fixed fee (hypothetical, before GST and expenses).
